strengths: Addresses an important evaluation gap: robustness of audio retrieval to query formulations beyond conventional captions, including exclusionary queries.

The multi-backbone evaluation across three datasets and several strong CLAP baselines provides useful empirical coverage. OEA is competitive in text-to-audio retrieval and consistently strong in text-to-text retrieval.
The explicit investigation of WavCaps overlap with AudioCaps and Clotho is valuable. Including MECAT as a nominally contamination-free evaluation set is a responsible methodological choice.
Separating ordinary recall from target–distractor discrimination is well motivated; paired hard negatives and rank-based diagnostics could support more informative evaluation than recall alone.
The paper reports efficiency measurements, detailed prompts, LoRA configuration, and per-dataset results, improving transparency.
weaknesses: The central UIQ benchmark is not adequately validated as a proxy for real user intent. It consists of synthetic transformations of existing captions, vocabulary and length are deliberately constrained, and only 15 clips (75 generated queries) are assessed by humans. The 675 ratings are repeated judgments of those same 75 queries, not broad benchmark coverage. This evidence cannot support general claims about real-world search behavior.

Benchmark construction is internally inconsistent. Section 3.2 states that positive queries must reuse caption vocabulary and remain within ±2 words of the original, but the disclosed generation prompt contains neither constraint and instead specifies independent absolute length ranges. The reported dataset sizes are also not reconciled with the number of clips and five query types.

Table 9 is presented as five queries for one audio example, yet its rows refer to incompatible content: dog barks, footsteps, and rain/wind. This concrete construction or reporting error substantially reduces confidence in the benchmark and its quality-control pipeline.

Hard-negative verification is underspecified: the number of reviewed pairs, sampling procedure, rejection rate, annotator counts, agreement, and final per-dataset pair counts are absent. Mining with MGA-CLAP may also bias comparisons involving MGA-CLAP, but this is not quantified.

Metric definitions and names are inconsistent. The main text reports TFR@10, whereas Appendix L defines TFR and TFR-HN@k; Table 17 again labels the latter TFR@10. HNSR and HNSR@k capture different events, while Table 4 combines HNSR@10 with R@5 values into an 'Avg UIQ,' producing an average of noncomparable metrics whose interpretation is unclear.

The claimed superiority in semantic understanding is stronger than the evidence. The key HNSR@10 advantage is 4.3 points, but no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variation across training seeds are reported. There are no controlled ablations separating shared-backbone effects, instruction tuning, model capacity, projection heads, or training data.

The broader empirical characterization is selective. M2D-CLAP has the best average UIQ score and wins three of four positive query types; OEA's text-to-audio gains are mixed. The claim of stronger generalization on Clotho relies mainly on variants explicitly trained with additional Clotho data, while MECAT gains are small and metric-dependent.

Text-to-text retrieval is a different caption-indexed setting and naturally favors a billion-parameter LLM text encoder over CLAP's smaller text tower. Without comparable strong text-embedding baselines, captioning quality/cost, or an end-to-end caption-generation evaluation, these results do not establish superiority for practical audio retrieval.

Reproducibility is currently insufficient for Findings: full datasets are deferred until publication, the apparent artifact link is missing, and important training details such as batch size, epoch/stage schedules, validation splits, seeds, and baseline checkpoint/evaluation procedures are not fully specified.

Overall, the model experiments are promising, but repairing and revalidating the benchmark, resolving metric inconsistencies, adding uncertainty and ablations, and releasing complete artifacts constitute important revisions before the contribution can be judged sound and reproducible. These changes appear feasible for a next-cycle resubmission.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant weakness in audio-text retrieval evaluation: conventional caption-style queries do not cover several plausible user-query formulations. The attempt to separate ordinary retrieval from hard-negative suppression is potentially useful.

The empirical study is broad, covering three multimodal LLM backbones, multiple CLAP baselines, three datasets, text-to-audio and text-to-text settings, several query formulations, and efficiency measurements.

The authors explicitly investigate training/evaluation contamination, identify substantial WavCaps overlap with AudioCaps and Clotho, apply blocklists, and include MECAT as a nominally leakage-free test set.

The architecture is clearly described, and the appendix provides useful details about pooling, LoRA configuration, projection heads, prompts, and metric definitions. The reported results support the narrower claim that retrieval adaptation makes multimodal LLM representations competitive with CLAP for text-to-audio retrieval and strong for text-to-text matching.
weaknesses: The central claim of superior negation or exclusion understanding is not established. Negative queries contain positive descriptions of the target as well as exclusions derived from a semantically dissimilar distractor. A model can rank the target above that distractor using only the positive target cues. The paper needs counterfactual controls such as removing the exclusion, replacing it with an irrelevant exclusion, reversing target and exclusion content, and testing whether rankings change in the intended direction.

The UIQ benchmark has weak ecological validity. Questions and imperatives are generated from rigid templates, positive queries are constrained to reuse caption wording and remain within two words of caption length, and the paper acknowledges that the resulting distribution does not reproduce real search queries averaging 1.8 tokens. Consequently, much of the benchmark tests superficial reformulation of existing captions rather than realistic user intent.

Human validation is inadequate for supporting a new benchmark. Only 15 audio examples—five per dataset—are evaluated, using an internal convenience sample. The criterion mainly asks whether a query makes sense relative to its source caption, not whether it is realistic, preserves every acoustic fact, or expresses the intended exclusion correctly. No inter-annotator reliability is reported. Human verification of hard negatives is even less reproducible: the sample size, number of annotators, protocol, rejection rate, and agreement are omitted.

Several conclusions overstate the evidence. OEA is not best on the aggregate UIQ retrieval score, and its main text-to-audio results trail M2D-CLAP on average. The claimed LLM semantic advantage rests mainly on a 4.3-point HNSR@10 difference and text-to-text retrieval, but the former lacks negation controls and uncertainty estimates, while the latter compares billion-parameter LLM text representations against smaller CLAP text encoders on a different, caption-indexed task. Neither establishes the asserted causal explanation about instruction pretraining or compositional attention.

Experimental uncertainty is missing: there are no multiple training seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or sensitivity analyses for hard-negative mining thresholds. This is particularly consequential because several headline differences are modest and the hard-negative benchmark is selected using MGA-CLAP and BGE embeddings.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the release claims. The full UIQ datasets are deferred until publication, links in the manuscript are absent, and important training details such as batch size, number of epochs or steps, weight decay, learning-rate schedule, checkpoint-selection specifics, random seeds, and exact baseline checkpoints are not given. Some references are also visibly incomplete or anonymized.

The paper would require an important but feasible revision: redesign the exclusion evaluation around controlled contrastive query pairs, conduct substantially larger and better documented human validation, report uncertainty across runs, and moderate claims about real-world robustness and semantic understanding. Until then, the evidence does not meet the soundness and reproducibility threshold for Findings.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: audio-retrieval robustness to conversational, reformulated, and exclusionary queries. The proposed UIQ framing is relevant to NLP and multimodal retrieval. Review based on the complete manuscript: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/56e247387f704b7fb33d47a8edfec3c1/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The empirical scope is substantial: three datasets, several strong CLAP baselines, three multimodal-LLM backbones, text-to-audio and text-to-text evaluation, negative-query analysis, and inference-efficiency measurements.

The paper reports results candidly: M2D-CLAP remains stronger on standard retrieval and several UIQ types, while OEA's advantages are concentrated in text-to-text retrieval, imperative queries, and selected hard-negative metrics.

The contamination analysis is valuable. Identifying AudioCaps-WavCaps and Clotho-WavCaps overlap, applying blocklists, and including MECAT as a cleaner benchmark improve the evaluation relative to common practice.

The narrower empirical conclusion that retrieval-adapted multimodal LLMs can be competitive with specialized CLAP models is reasonably supported across multiple backbones. The benchmark, prompts, and checkpoints could also become useful community resources if released and documented fully.
weaknesses: The central UIQ benchmark is not validated rigorously enough for a clear Findings recommendation. It is generated by one proprietary LLM, while human evaluation covers only 15 clips and asks whether a query "makes sense" relative to a caption—not whether it resembles genuine user behavior or preserves the exact retrieval intent. Inter-annotator agreement is not reported, and comparison with real search logs is largely limited to token length.

There are serious internal inconsistencies in benchmark documentation. Section 3.2.2 says positive queries reuse caption vocabulary and remain within ±2 words of the source, but the disclosed generation prompt contains neither constraint and instead specifies different absolute length ranges. Moreover, Table 9 claims to show five queries for one audio clip, yet its examples describe mutually incompatible events such as dog barks, footsteps, and heavy rain. These issues undermine reproducibility and confidence in the reported benchmark.

The hard-negative construction is insufficiently specified and validated. Acoustic and semantic thresholds are omitted, and the paper says only that annotators inspected "sampled" pairs, without the sample size, acceptance rate, annotation protocol, or agreement. Because HNSR and related conclusions depend directly on pair quality, this is a central soundness concern.

No confidence intervals, significance tests, multiple-seed results, or per-dataset negative-query results are provided. The highlighted advantage is only 4.3 points on HNSR@10, and different OEA variants attain the best HNSR, TFR, and TFR@10 values. The evidence therefore does not justify describing a uniformly or substantially superior discrimination capability.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed benefit of an LLM backbone. OEA and CLAP systems differ in parameter count, pretraining, architecture, and training data; there is no controlled shared-versus-dual-encoder ablation or component ablation. The proposed explanations involving instruction following, compositional attention, and negation exposure remain hypotheses.

The strong text-to-text results are only indirect evidence for audio retrieval: they assume that each audio item has already been converted into a suitable caption, but no end-to-end captioning-and-retrieval pipeline is evaluated. Performance may reflect ordinary text embedding quality rather than improved audio-language alignment.

Important reproducibility details remain missing, including batch sizes, epochs or step counts, learning-rate assignment by model/stage, seeds, exact baseline checkpoints, final post-blocklist training counts, and complete threshold settings. The full benchmark is also deferred until publication and depends on proprietary generation models.

Overall, this is a promising and potentially useful submission, but unresolved benchmark-integrity, validation, statistical-evidence, and reproducibility concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation in its current form. These appear addressable with a carefully documented regeneration/audit, stronger human validation, controlled ablations, and uncertainty analysis.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant weakness in audio-text retrieval evaluation: standard caption queries poorly represent the range of formulations users may employ. The proposed question, imperative, keyphrase, paraphrase, and exclusionary query categories provide a useful starting taxonomy.

Evaluation spans three datasets, several strong CLAP baselines, and three multimodal-LLM backbones. The leakage analysis is unusually valuable, and including MECAT partially mitigates the serious AudioCaps/Clotho overlap with WavCaps.

OEA achieves competitive text-to-audio retrieval and consistently strong imperative-query results. The post-hoc analyses also improve the paper by correcting an overly simple negation-understanding explanation: the evidence instead suggests that audio-side separation is important and that word-order sensitivity is shared by CLAP encoders.

The paper is generally clear and candid about several limitations, including computational cost, synthetic-query bias, contaminated benchmarks, hard-negative-miner dependence, and the fact that exclusion clauses actually hurt every evaluated model.
weaknesses: The central claim that UIQs reflect real-world search behavior is not adequately validated. All queries are generated by one LLM under highly constrained templates and caption-grounded vocabulary, while only 15 clips—75 distinct queries, roughly 0.6% of the released benchmark—receive human evaluation. The annotation question measures compatibility with a source caption, not realism relative to actual user queries. No comparison to search logs or naturally collected queries is provided, despite cited evidence that real audio queries average only 1.8 tokens.

The benchmark construction is insufficiently reproducible. Exact acoustic and semantic filtering thresholds are omitted; the human calibration sample size, annotator details, judgments, and agreement are not reported; and the relationship between the stated 13,053 query counts, mined pairs, and per-type examples is unclear. Training details also omit important quantities such as batch sizes, stage lengths, random seeds, and run-to-run variation.

The headline text-to-text contribution is weakly supported. The protocol is underspecified—particularly how gallery captions are formed and separated from queries—and it does not evaluate the claimed end-to-end audio-captioning retrieval pipeline. Comparing a billion-parameter LLM encoder only against CLAP text branches, without strong dedicated text-embedding baselines such as E5 or BGE, cannot establish dominant text retrieval. This result is also only indirectly relevant to audio retrieval.

The hard-negative claims overstate the evidence. HNSR@k combines target retrieval with hard-negative suppression, so differences cannot be attributed solely to exclusion understanding. Results are inconsistent across metrics and variants: Robust-CLAP exceeds the highlighted OEA-Qwen7B (+Cl) in mean delta-rank, while the best HNSR@10 and TFR@10 improvements come from different OEA variants. The paper selectively combines these best-family results in its headline claims.

No uncertainty or significance analysis is given for the main retrieval and discrimination comparisons, apparently based on single runs. A 4.3-point HNSR@10 improvement is therefore difficult to assess, especially after selecting among six OEA variants and averaging heterogeneous datasets. Statistical tests are confined to post-hoc mechanism analyses.

Baseline comparability remains uncertain because training corpora and contamination differ across systems. Although the authors block overlapping WavCaps examples for OEA, the pretrained baselines may have seen evaluation audio. Conversely, the assertion that MECAT is truly leakage-free is stronger than source provenance and embedding/filename checks justify for web-derived data.

The architectural contribution is incremental: standard contrastive learning, LoRA, pooling, and projection heads are applied to existing native-audio multimodal models, including an embedding-oriented Nemotron backbone. The strongest empirical novelty is therefore the benchmark, whose current validation and documentation are not yet strong enough to support a Findings recommendation. A next-cycle revision should validate on substantially more human-authored or logged queries, fully specify construction and training, add text-embedding and end-to-end captioning baselines, report repeated-run uncertainty, and temper or disentangle the exclusionary claims.

strengths: The manuscript is clearly organized and motivates evaluating audio retrieval beyond caption-style queries. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/b4b1ad541cfc484f940d8538c85547bb/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Evaluation covers several backbones, datasets, CLAP baselines, query formulations, and efficiency measurements. The authors also investigate overlap between WavCaps and common evaluation sets and apply blocklists.
Distinguishing ordinary recall from target-versus-hard-negative behavior is useful, and reporting HNSR, rank gaps, and stricter target-first measures exposes behavior hidden by R@k alone.

The post-hoc ablations are unusually candid: they test audio-space separation, removal of the exclusion clause, word-order shuffling, and cross-model controls, substantially qualifying the initial mechanism hypothesis.
weaknesses: The central claim of superior exclusionary-query understanding is not supported by the paper's own ablations. Removing the exclusion clause improves suppression for every model, while OEA's advantage is attributed chiefly to query-independent audio-space separation. This demonstrates a better embedding geometry, not understanding of what the user requests to exclude.

The proposed UIQs are weak proxies for real user intent. They are generated by one LLM under rigid templates, constrained to reuse caption vocabulary and roughly caption length, even though the motivating evidence says real audio searches average 1.8 tokens. The benchmark therefore evaluates controlled synthetic transformations more directly than realistic search behavior.

Benchmark validation is inadequate: only 75 of 13,053 queries are examined, sample selection is unspecified, and the criterion asks merely whether a query makes sense relative to its source caption rather than whether it is natural, representative, or preserves retrieval intent. Annotator details and a standard inter-annotator reliability analysis are absent, and the paper inconsistently characterizes r=0.89 as human-LLM agreement and inter-annotator agreement.

The headline text-to-text experiment is insufficiently defined. The paper describes it as simulating an audio-captioning pipeline but specifies neither a captioning model nor caption-generation protocol, caption gallery construction, or handling of multiple reference captions. If ground-truth or source captions are used, the experiment is effectively oracle text matching and does not support claims about a practical caption-based audio retrieval system.

Primary retrieval comparisons appear to be single runs: there are no random-seed repetitions, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the headline gains. Several conclusions rely on small differences and selectively highlight different OEA variants across metrics, so robustness is unclear.

The hard-negative benchmark is not reproducible from the manuscript. Acoustic and semantic thresholds are not reported, and the human calibration lacks sample counts, annotator protocol, agreement, and quantitative results. Mining with MGA-CLAP also induces model-dependent selection bias that the subsequent filtering does not eliminate.

The claim that MECAT is leakage-free is too strong. Dataset provenance alone cannot establish absence of overlap between web-video corpora, the stated embedding and filename checks are not documented quantitatively, and the pretraining data of the large multimodal backbones are not audited. Comparability of baseline training exposure is also not established.

Training details are incomplete despite the release claim: batch sizes, stage durations, sampling ratios, early-stopping settings, seeds, exact learning-rate assignment, final filtered dataset sizes, and computational training requirements are missing. Together with incomplete bibliographic entries such as 'Anonymous Wu and 1 others,' this falls short of a clearly reproducible contribution.

Overall, the architecture is a fairly direct combination of frozen native-audio LLM backbones, LoRA, mean pooling, projection heads, and contrastive learning. Given that standard UIQ retrieval is not improved overall and the exclusion interpretation is undermined by the ablations, the present evidence does not establish a sound Findings-level contribution. A next-cycle revision could become viable with realistic human queries, fully specified benchmark construction, a non-oracle T2T pipeline, repeated-run statistics, and claims aligned with what the negation controls actually show.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant weakness in audio-text retrieval evaluation: conventional benchmarks rely heavily on caption-style queries. The five query formulations and exclusion-focused metrics provide a useful starting point for broader robustness evaluation. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/befd54a3c34244dc9945b09edd558628/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical study is broad: it covers three datasets, four CLAP baselines, three multimodal-LLM backbones, text-to-audio and text-to-text settings, several query types, and efficiency measurements. The leakage analysis and inclusion of MECAT as a cleaner evaluation set are especially valuable.

OEA obtains strong and consistent text-to-text results and competitive text-to-audio performance. Its best-supported advantage is improved separation of target and confusable audio embeddings, including statistically tested comparisons against M2D-CLAP.

The mechanism analysis is unusually candid. The authors show that exclusion clauses actually hurt every evaluated model, that order sensitivity is shared with CLAP encoders, and that OEA's hard-negative advantage chiefly arises from its audio representation rather than a uniquely strong understanding of negation.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and relevant to both multimodal NLP and information retrieval.
weaknesses: The framing sometimes overstates semantic or complex-query understanding. HNSR improvements can result from query-independent separation in the audio embedding space, and the authors' own ablations show that removing the exclusion clause improves suppression. Thus, the results do not demonstrate successful semantic execution of exclusion instructions.

The ecological validity of UIQ is limited. Queries are generated by one LLM from benchmark captions, constrained to reuse caption vocabulary and remain within plus or minus two words of the original length. This controlled transformation does not closely reflect the cited real-world audio queries averaging 1.8 tokens, and no evaluation on actual user queries or search logs is provided.

Benchmark validation covers only 75 of 13,053 queries. The reported criterion asks whether a query makes sense relative to a caption, not whether it resembles authentic search behavior or accurately distinguishes the target from its paired hard negative. Inter-annotator reliability is also insufficiently reported; the highlighted correlation appears to concern human-LLM agreement rather than agreement among annotators.

The hard-negative benchmark is partly model-defined: candidates are mined with MGA-CLAP and filtered through caption embeddings, while negative queries are generated using both target and distractor captions. Sample-based threshold calibration helps but does not establish the quality of every pair or coverage of perceptually important confusions.

The practical text-to-text claim is not fully substantiated. The evaluation appears to retrieve dataset caption text, including human-authored captions for AudioCaps and Clotho, rather than captions produced by a specified automatic audio-captioning pipeline. Consequently, the large T2T gains do not directly demonstrate end-to-end caption-based audio retrieval performance.

Reproducibility is weaker than the release claim suggests: the manuscript provides no accessible artifact location and omits consequential details such as batch sizes, stage schedules, random-seed variation, and uncertainty or significance tests for the main retrieval comparisons. Baseline contamination and training-data comparability are also not fully controlled.

Overall, this is a useful and mostly sound Findings-level contribution, but the synthetic benchmark's limited validation and the mismatch between discrimination gains and genuine exclusion understanding prevent a main-conference recommendation.
